title: First Atmosphere Detected on a Rocky Planet in the Habitable Zone—A Game Changer for Alien Life Hunt
summary:
For decades, astronomers have wondered: do rocky planets in other solar systems have atmospheres? Now, we have a thrilling answer. For the first time, scientists have confirmed an atmosphere on a rocky exoplanet orbiting within the habitable zone—the region where temperatures could allow liquid water, a key ingredient for life. The planet, LHS 1140 b, is a super-Earth about 48 light-years away, with 5.6 times Earth’s mass. It’s a chilly minus 53°F on the surface, but an atmosphere could trap heat and make it more hospitable.

The breakthrough, published July 16 in Science, didn’t come from seeing the atmosphere directly. Instead, researchers used the WINERED spectrograph on Chile’s Magellan Clay Telescope to catch the planet transiting its star. As starlight filtered through the planet’s edge, they spotted a telltale dip in infrared light at a wavelength blocked by helium—clear evidence of gas escaping into space. “It’s absolutely exciting,” said Edward Schwieterman, an astrobiologist at UC Riverside. “We are getting closer to studying the atmospheres of worlds that could plausibly harbor life.”

What makes this detection even more compelling is the contrast with a neighboring planet. On the same night in September 2024, the team observed LHS 1140 c, a smaller, hotter world that orbits much closer to the star and receives five times the radiation. It showed no helium signal, suggesting its atmosphere was stripped away long ago. LHS 1140 b, however, has held onto its gaseous envelope for at least 3.1 billion years, despite the star’s harsh radiation. This challenges assumptions that red dwarf stars inevitably destroy atmospheres.

But don’t pack your bags yet. The helium reveals only the upper atmosphere; we still don’t know if it contains oxygen, water vapor, or other life-friendly gases. “The study demonstrates that, at least in some cases, we will be able to begin characterizing the atmospheres of potentially habitable planets,” Schwieterman added. Future telescopes, like the Habitable Worlds Observatory, could search for biosignatures—chemical signs of life. For now, this discovery is a monumental step, proving that some rocky worlds can cling to their air, and with it, the potential for life.
why_it_matters: This discovery moves us closer to answering whether we are alone in the universe, a question that shapes our understanding of our place and future exploration.

background_read: Red dwarf stars, also called M dwarfs, make up about 70% of the stars in the Milky Way and often host rocky planets in their habitable zones.
Earlier studies suggested that the intense radiation from such stars would quickly strip away atmospheres, leaving planets barren.
LHS 1140 b, located 48 light-years away in the constellation Cetus, orbits a red dwarf and was studied by Edward Schwieterman (an astrobiologist at the University of California, Riverside).
The team used the WINERED spectrograph on the Magellan Clay Telescope in Chile, an instrument that detects infrared light, to catch the planet passing in front of its star.
The detection of escaping helium challenges the old assumption and offers hope that planets around the galaxy's most common stars could hold onto life-friendly air.
The Habitable Worlds Observatory, a planned NASA space telescope, aims to search for biosignatures—tell-tale chemical markers like oxygen—once it launches in the 2040s.

perspectives.description: Astrobiologists are thrilled because this proves rocky planets around red dwarfs can retain atmospheres, vastly expanding the number of worlds that might support life. It increases the chances that we are not alone.

Some researchers caution that a thin escaping helium signal doesn’t guarantee a surface habitable for humans; red dwarfs still emit deadly flares and the planet’s cold temperature may require a thick greenhouse effect that may not exist.

The discovery forces a re-examination of stellar evolution models that predicted small, close-in planets would lose their atmospheres early. It suggests that atmospheric retention timescales are more variable than thought, and many previously dismissed planets deserve a second look.

Upcoming telescopes like the Habitable Worlds Observatory, scheduled for the 2040s, could detect biosignatures such as oxygen and methane. If found, it would revolutionize biology and our philosophical understanding of life’s uniqueness.
